label: bm-building-physics-standards
topic: What a building element must pass: moisture, fire, durability, tests (polymer shading or cladding, England-focused)
summary: What a polymer shading or cladding element has to pass, and what a desk-scale proof of concept can skip, in England. Law: Regulation 7(1) needs 'adequate and proper materials'; for buildings with a storey at 18 m or more containing dwellings, institutions or residential rooms, Regulation 7(2) needs Euroclass A2-s1,d0 or A1 for everything in external walls and attachments, and Approved Document B applies that to shading slats above 4.5 m. Approved Document 7 para 1.27 is the nearest wording for a humidity-responsive material: residual properties must be estimable and adequate for the expected life. Fire: Euroclass needs large end-use specimens (SBI wings 1.5 m tall, 3 specimens); a desk print cannot be classified. Formlabs publishes only UL 94 (HB at 3 mm for the 9 of 25 data sheets scanned that give a rating; V-0 at 3 mm only for Flame Retardant Resin, falling to HB at 1.5 mm), and UL 94 is not in Approved Document B. Ageing: no standard sets pass marks; the practice is ISO 4892 xenon or UV exposure (Cheng 2024: 96 h; Formlabs nylon: 1000 h, within 4-6 % in strength, elongation down 15-17 %), with one conflicting source (Pilipovic 2022: modulus roughly halved on PA 2200). Humidity-responsive elements have no standard; the literature uses climate-chamber RH cycling (170 cycles in 1020 h) across several temperatures. New beyond earlier agents: Formlabs does publish ageing and creep graphs for some resins (values unreadable); EN ISO 62 is the method for the missing water diffusivity; and the CTE gap between Rigid 10K and Tough 1000 gives a thermal differential strain (0.45-0.51 % over 40 K) larger than the estimated 0.2 % hygroscopic strain. Requirement, recommendation and unknown are tagged in each finding. Scotland, Northern Ireland, UKCA marking, BS 8414 and the fire safety order were not researched.
lay_summary: A building part has to survive fire, sun, rain, heat and years of use, and the rules are strict mostly for tall homes. In England, on a building 18 metres or higher where people sleep, shading slats must be close to non-burning, which ordinary printed plastic is very unlikely to be. A small printed model on a desk is not a building part, so those rules do not apply to it, but it still should not claim to be fire-safe or weatherproof. Nobody has written a test standard for a panel that bends when the air gets damp; researchers invent their own, such as 170 damp-and-dry cycles in a chamber. We also found a trap: warming the same two-plastic strip can bend it more than the damp air does, like a metal-and-brass thermostat strip. So the first honest experiment is to measure damp and heat effects separately.

findings.claim: REQUIREMENT (England): building work must use 'adequate and proper materials' appropriate for the circumstances of use. This is the only durability-type duty that applies to every building element regardless of height; it names no test.
findings.evidence_quote: with adequate and proper materials which— (i) are appropriate for the circumstances in which they are used

findings.claim: REQUIREMENT (England): in a 'relevant building' every material that becomes part of an external wall or a specified attachment must be Euroclass A2-s1,d0 or A1.
findings.evidence_quote: materials which become part of an external wall, or specified attachment, of a relevant building are of European Classification A2-s1, d0 or A1

findings.claim: REQUIREMENT (England): a 'relevant building' has a storey at least 18 m above ground level and contains dwellings, an institution or a room for residential purposes.
findings.evidence_quote: a building with a storey (not including roof-top plant areas or any storey consisting exclusively of plant rooms) at least 18 metres above ground level

findings.claim: REQUIREMENT (England): the Regulation 7(3)(ha) exemption for solar-shading components explicitly excludes the parts whose job is to give shade, so slats and fins of a shading device are NOT exempt from the A2-s1,d0 rule.
findings.evidence_quote: components associated with a solar shading device excluding components whose primary function is to provide shade or deflect sunlight such as the awning curtain or slats

findings.claim: GUIDANCE (Approved Document B vol 2): in a relevant building the curtain and/or slats of a solar shading device must achieve class A1 or A2-s1,d0.
findings.evidence_quote: Regulation 7(2) requires that the curtain and or slats of solar shading devices in a relevant building (as defined in regulation 7(4)) achieve class A1 or A2-s1, d0.

findings.claim: GUIDANCE (Approved Document B vol 2): solar shading devices installed up to 4.5 m above ground level are not required to meet Regulation 7(2). So a low shading element on a tall residential building is outside the A2-s1,d0 rule, but is not thereby outside all fire guidance.
findings.evidence_quote: Solar shading devices installed up to 4.5m above ground level are not required to meet the requirements of regulation 7(2).

findings.claim: GUIDANCE: ADB says the 'specified attachment' definition includes solar shading.
findings.evidence_quote: External walls and specified attachments are defined in regulation 2(6) and these definitions include any parts of the external wall as well as balconies, solar panels and solar shading.

findings.claim: GUIDANCE (ADB Table 12.1): for relevant buildings the external-surface class is A2-s1,d0 or better at any distance from the boundary; for other residential buildings over 11 m it is also A2-s1,d0 or better. Other building types get B-s3,d2 or C-s3,d2 depending on height and boundary distance. I could not confirm from the text whether Table 12.1 (written for 'external surfaces of external walls') is meant to apply to a free-standing shading device on a building under 18 m.
findings.evidence_quote: More than 11m Class A2-s1, d0(2) or better Class A2-s1, d0(2) or better

findings.claim: GUIDANCE: for buildings that are not relevant buildings, ADB offers a second route: meet BRE report BR 135 using full-scale BS 8414-1/-2 test data. I did not read BR 135 or BS 8414.
findings.evidence_quote: Meet the performance criteria given in BRE report BR 135 for external walls using full-scale test data from BS 8414-1 or BS 8414-2.

findings.claim: GUIDANCE: ADB no longer uses national classes (the 2025 amendments removed them), and says a product cannot assume a European class unless it has been tested accordingly.
findings.evidence_quote: therefore products cannot typically assume a European class unless they have been tested accordingly.

findings.claim: GUIDANCE (Approved Document 7): 'materials that are susceptible to changes in their properties' are allowed if the residual properties can be estimated at the time of incorporation and are shown adequate for the expected life of the building. This is the closest England-wide wording to a humidity-responsive material, and it demands a predicted end-of-life property estimate.
findings.evidence_quote: Materials that are susceptible to changes in their properties may be used in building work and will meet the requirements of the regulations if the residual properties, including the structural properties, meet both of the following conditions.

findings.claim: GUIDANCE (Approved Document 7): the second condition is that residual properties are shown adequate for the building to perform its function for the expected life of the building.
findings.evidence_quote: Residual properties are shown to be adequate for the building to perform the function for which it is intended, for the expected life of the building.

findings.claim: GUIDANCE (Approved Document 7): a short-lived material that can be inspected and replaced may be acceptable if failure would not seriously endanger people. This is the legitimate route for a replaceable, low-consequence shading element.
findings.evidence_quote: A short-lived material which is readily accessible for inspection, maintenance and replacement may meet the requirements of the regulations if the consequences of failure are not likely to be serious

findings.claim: GUIDANCE (Approved Document 7): where no harmonised European standard exists, tests, calculations or other means may demonstrate fitness, and past experience in an existing building may also show it. Test labs accredited by UKAS or equivalent are the stated way to make tests reliable.
findings.evidence_quote: Where there is no relevant harmonised European standard, tests, calculations or other means may be used to demonstrate that the material can perform the function for which it is intended.

findings.claim: REQUIREMENT (England, Part C, C2): walls must protect the building and its users from harmful effects of precipitation including wind-driven spray, and interstitial and surface condensation. ADB-C paragraph 5.7 allows an 'impervious or weather-resisting cladding' as one way to do it. A shading fin hung outside a weatherproof wall is not itself the rain barrier (my inference); a cladding panel is.
findings.evidence_quote: (b) precipitation including wind-driven spray;

findings.claim: GUIDANCE/EXEMPTION (England): Schedule 2 of the Building Regulations 2010 lists 'Temporary buildings', buildings not intended to remain where erected for more than 28 days, as an exempt class. Whether a shading attachment to an existing building counts as a temporary building is NOT CONFIRMED.
findings.evidence_quote: Temporary buildings E+W A building which is not intended to remain where it is erected for more than 28 days.

findings.claim: INFERENCE: Approved Document 7 defines 'building work' as erection or extension of a building, provision of a controlled service or fitting, or material alteration. A desk-scale printed demonstrator that is not installed on a building is not building work and so sits outside the Building Regulations altogether.
findings.evidence_quote: Building work includes: a. the erection or extension of a building

findings.claim: INFERENCE: the Construction Products Regulation defines a construction product as one placed on the market for incorporation in a permanent manner in construction works. A desk-scale object that is never sold for installation is outside it; a product offered to an architecture practice for a façade would be inside it. I read the EU text; the retained UK version (and UKCA marking) was NOT read.
findings.evidence_quote: ‘construction product’ means any product or kit which is produced and placed on the market for incorporation in a permanent manner in construction works

findings.claim: REQUIREMENT (EU CPR Art 5(a)): where a product is covered by a harmonised standard, the manufacturer may skip the declaration of performance for a one-off, custom-made, non-series product installed in a single identified work, but the manufacturer stays responsible for safe incorporation under national rules. This does not remove national requirements such as Regulation 7.
findings.evidence_quote: the construction product is individually manufactured or custom-made in a non-series process in response to a specific order, and installed in a single identified construction work

findings.claim: REQUIREMENT (EU CPR Annex I): construction works must meet the basic requirements, which include limiting the generation and spread of fire and smoke, 'for an economically reasonable working life', subject to normal maintenance. The Regulation does not give a number of years.
findings.evidence_quote: Subject to normal maintenance, construction works must satisfy these basic requirements for construction works for an economically reasonable working life.

findings.claim: REQUIREMENT (EU classification regulation 2016/364): reaction to fire is classified A1, A2, B, C, D, E, F, with smoke s1-s3 and droplets d0-d2 added. Class A2 needs either a non-combustibility result (ISO 1182: furnace temperature rise at most 50 C, mass loss at most 50 %, flaming at most 20 s) or a gross heat of combustion (ISO 1716) of at most 3.0 MJ/kg for the product, AND an SBI test.
findings.evidence_quote: A2 EN ISO 1182 ( 2 ) ; or ΔΤ ≤ 50 °C; and Δm ≤ 50 %; and t f ≤ 20 s EN ISO 1716; and PCS ≤ 3,0 MJkg – 1 ( 2 )
findings.value: PCS <= 3.0 MJ/kg (homogeneous product or substantial component; 4.0 MJ/m2 for non-substantial layers)

findings.claim: Class B needs an SBI result with FIGRA at most 120 W/s and total heat release (600 s) at most 7.5 MJ, plus a small-flame test.
findings.evidence_quote: B EN 13823 (SBI); and FIGRA ≤ 120 Ws – 1 ; and LFS < edge of specimen; and THR 600s ≤ 7,5 MJ

findings.claim: Class E needs only the small-flame test EN ISO 11925-2 (15 s exposure, flame spread at most 150 mm within 20 s).
findings.evidence_quote: E EN ISO 11925-2 ( 9 ) : Exposure = 15 s Fs ≤ 150 mm within 20 s

findings.claim: Smoke classes: s1 = SMOGRA at most 30 m2/s2 and TSP600s at most 50 m2; s2 = at most 180 and 200; s3 = otherwise.
findings.evidence_quote: s1 = SMOGRA ≤ 30m 2 s – 2 and TSP 600s ≤ 50m 2 ; s2 = SMOGRA ≤ 180m 2 s – 2 and TSP 600s ≤ 200m 2 ; s3 = not s1 or s2.

findings.claim: Droplet classes: d0 = no flaming droplets/particles in the SBI within 600 s; d1 = none persisting over 10 s; d2 = otherwise. Ignition of the paper in the small-flame test gives d2.
findings.evidence_quote: d0 = No flaming droplets/particles in EN 13823 (SBI) within 600s; d1 = No flaming droplets/particles persisting longer than 10s in EN 13823 (SBI) within 600s; d2 = not d0 or d1

findings.claim: EN 13501-1 is the classification procedure for all construction products, 'considered in relation to their end use application'.
findings.evidence_quote: This document provides the reaction to fire classification procedure for all construction products, including products incorporated within building elements

findings.claim: Test-house description of class E: such products 'may quickly lead to a flash-over situation, possibly within the first two minutes' of the reference scenario.
findings.evidence_quote: Class E products may quickly lead to a flash-over situation, possibly within the first two minutes of the reference scenario test

findings.claim: The SBI (EN 13823) test needs a corner of two wings: long wing 495 mm x 1500 mm and a short wing of (1000 + product thickness) mm x 1500 mm, and at least 3 specimens, under a 30 kW burner. A desk-scale printed object cannot be classified with it.
findings.evidence_quote: Long wing: 495 mm x 1500 mm
findings.value: 495 x 1500 mm and (1000+t) x 1500 mm; >= 3 specimens

findings.claim: The SBI specimens 'shall be representative of the product as placed in the market or in its end-use application, including both vertical and horizontal joints'.
findings.evidence_quote: Test specimens shall be representative of the product as placed in the market or in its end-use application, including both vertical and horizontal joints, as far as possible.

findings.claim: At one accredited lab the SBI report takes about 3-4 weeks after the specimens arrive. This is a lab statement, not a standard.
findings.evidence_quote: Normally it will take about 3-4 weeks from when we have received the test specimens until the test report is finished.

findings.claim: ISO 1182 non-combustibility uses small cylinders 45 mm diameter x 50 mm high, five parallel tests. These fit inside a Form 4 build, so a printed coupon CAN legitimately be screened for A1/A2 non-combustibility at desk scale (RECOMMENDATION; the result would not be a classification).
findings.evidence_quote: The specimens are cylindrical with diameter 45 mm and height 50 mm.

findings.claim: ISO 1716 (bomb calorimeter, gross heat of combustion) is 'intended to be applied to solid products' and needs only a small sample, so it is the other desk-scale fire screen. I could not fetch a verified polymer value to compare with the 3.0 MJ/kg A2 limit (FAA report server returned 503).

A European façade reference fire scenario does not exist; in a worked European Technical Assessment (ETA 20/0062, EAD 090062-00-0404) 'Façade fire performance' is 'No performance determined' and the kit is classed by its worst component. National façade fire tests (for England, BS 8414/BR 135) sit on top of component classes.
findings.evidence_quote: A European reference fire scenario has not been laid down for facades.

findings.claim: In that ETA the reaction to fire of the kit is assessed from the components of the kit.
findings.evidence_quote: the reaction to fire of the kit is assessed by considering the reaction to fire of the components of the kit

findings.claim: ABSENCE (verified by search of the saved file): the string 'UL 94' / 'UL94' does not occur in the Approved Document B volume 2 text I downloaded (0 matches). UL 94 is the only flammability rating Formlabs publishes, so Formlabs flammability data cannot be translated into an ADB class.

Formlabs TDS flammability rating is UL 94 HB at 3 mm for Rigid 10K (post-cured) and for Nylon 12, Nylon 11, Nylon 12 GF, Nylon 12 Tough and Nylon 12 White; Tough 1000, 1500 V2 and 2000 V2 read 'Not Tested' (green) and 'HB' (post-cured). Of the 25 Formlabs TDS files scanned only these 9 report any UL 94 rating; the other 16 (Rigid 4000, Durable, Flexible, Silicone, Clear, Grey, High Temp, ESD, BioMed, Nylon 11 CF, TPU 90A) state none.
findings.evidence_quote: Testing Standard Rating UL 94 Section 7 HB

findings.claim: The same HB-at-3-mm statement for Rigid 10K is in its TDS (Rigid 10K also lists ASTM E662 smoke density).
findings.evidence_quote: UL 94 Section 7 (3 mm) HB

findings.claim: Formlabs Flame Retardant Resin (Form 4 family compatible) is rated UL 94 V-0 at 3 mm, V-1 at 2.5 mm and only HB at 1.5 mm, so the rating is thickness dependent and a thin hygromorph flap (0.2-2 mm) would not carry V-0.
Flame Retardant Resin: HDT 83 C at 1.8 MPa when post-cured at 80 C/120 min; Formlabs says parts suit 'indoor and industrial environments'. It makes no outdoor or UV claim on the page read.
findings.evidence_quote: perform well long-term in indoor and industrial environments with high temperatures or ignition sources

findings.claim: The Flame Retardant Resin also lists FAR 25.853 Appendix F Part I (12 s vertical burn, pass at 2.5 mm). That is an aircraft-interior test, not a building test.
findings.evidence_quote: FAR 25.853 Appendix F, Part I (a) (1) (ii)12 seconds Vertical Burn Pass (2.5mm)

findings.claim: NOT CONFIRMED: I found no EN 13501-1 class for any Formlabs resin or powder, for printed PLA modules by the architecture practice, or for any printed hygromorph. The practice states only that interior PLA is 'compounded with fireproof materials' (project record: spec-partner-architecture.json).

ABSENCE (grep of full texts): the words 'fire' and 'flame' do not occur in the full text of the two principal humidity-responsive-façade papers (Cheng 2024; Rueggeberg and Burgert 2015) read in this run. Fire behaviour of these elements is untested in the literature I could access.

Standard: EN ISO 4892-2 exposes plastics to xenon-arc light with moisture to reproduce daylight (or daylight through window glass) weathering; EN ISO 4892-3 does the same with fluorescent UV lamps, heat and water. Neither sets pass/fail limits; 'specimen preparation and evaluation of the results are covered in other standards'.
findings.evidence_quote: specifies methods for exposing specimens to xenon-arc light in the presence of moisture to reproduce the weathering effects (temperature, humidity and/or wetting)

findings.claim: EN ISO 4892-3 (fluorescent UV) scope.
findings.evidence_quote: specifies methods for exposing specimens to fluorescent UV radiation, heat and water in apparatus designed to simulate the weathering effects

findings.claim: ISO/TS 24110:2026, published 2026-04-21, describes exposing specimens to artificial UV radiation in combination with a creep load, using ISO 899-1 for the creep test. It is the first standard I found that couples UV and sustained load, which is the real condition of a hanging shading fin. Technical Specification, not a full standard; full text paywalled and unread.
findings.evidence_quote: This document describes a test method of exposing specimens to artificial UV radiation in combination with a creep load. This method uses UV radiation source and ISO 899-1 for the tensile creep test.

findings.claim: Cheng et al. 2024 (4D-printed cellulose-composite/ASA shading bilayers) exposed bilayers 'according to the DIN EN ISO 4892-2/-3 UV standard' for only 96 h at 60 C dry heat (4 days), then compared curvature at 30 % and 90 % RH with an unexposed control.
findings.evidence_quote: The specimens were exposed to the UV light source at a dry heat of 60 ∘ C for 96 hours

findings.claim: The restricting layer in that work, ASA, was chosen 'for its UV-resistant properties': the passive layer was picked for UV resistance, not only for stiffness.
findings.evidence_quote: filament was chosen for its UV-resistant properties

findings.claim: Formlabs published an accelerated-weathering study of Nylon 12 Powder and Nylon 12 Tough Powder: ASTM D4329-21 Cycle A, 1000 h, run by an independent lab, tensile bars printed on Fuse. The page is undated.
findings.evidence_quote: tested under ASTM D4329-21, Cycle A, using Xenon arc exposure for 1000 hours

findings.claim: Result after 1000 h: Nylon 12 UTS 50.8 -> 48.9 MPa (-3.7 %), modulus 1832 -> 1764 MPa (-3.7 %), elongation 9.78 -> 8.13 % (-16.9 %); colour change dE00 0.60.
findings.evidence_quote: Nylon 12 Powder Exposure Time 0 hrs 1,000 hrs Change Ultimate Tensile Strength 50.8 MPa 48.9 MPa -3.7% Tensile Modulus 1832 MPa 1764 MPa -3.7% Elongation at Break (X/Y) 9.78% 8.13% -16.9%
Nylon 12 Tough Powder Exposure Time 0 hrs 1,000 hrs Change Ultimate Tensile Strength 40.5 MPa 38 MPa -6.1% Tensile Modulus 1399 MPa 1402 MPa 0.2% Elongation at Break (X/Y) 19.2% 16.4% -14.7%

findings.claim: Formlabs states its own pass rule: 'less than 10% change in modulus and strength, and less than 20% change in elongation', and admits 'there is no single universal standard' for acceptable property change. The 10/20 % rule is an industry habit, not a building-standard requirement.
findings.evidence_quote: the industry-accepted definition of stability can typically be defined as less than 10% change in modulus and strength, and less than 20% change in elongation

findings.claim: DISAGREEMENT between sources on PA12 UV ageing. Formlabs (above): modulus -3.7 %, elongation -16.9 % after 1000 h D4329 with condensation cycles. Pilipovic et al. 2022 (EOS PA 2200 on an EOS Formiga P100, ISO 4892 solar box, 550 W/m2 300-800 nm, 65 C, no wetting, 1000 h): strain at break down 70-90 % in two orientations, and after natural weathering modulus 'reduced by almost half'. Different powder, machine, exposure and orientation; I cannot say which is right for a Fuse-printed part, and neither tested humidity-driven bending.
findings.evidence_quote: Tensile strength was reduced only by 10%, whereas strain and tensile modulus in orientation Lxy and Pxy were reduced by almost half the value in comparison to the situation before exposure to weathering conditions.
findings.value: Formlabs -3.7 % modulus vs Pilipovic ~ -50 % modulus (natural weathering, 120 d)

findings.claim: Pilipovic 2022 also says '1 h of laboratory testing in a UV chamber corresponds to 24 h of natural exposure' and so 1000 h = 2.8 years. Formlabs makes no such equivalence and its resin TDS warns that accelerated testing 'cannot fully represent all aging conditions'. The conversion factor is therefore contested and not a standard.
findings.evidence_quote: 1 h of laboratory testing in a UV chamber corresponds to 24 h of natural exposure to UV light

findings.claim: Earlier agent's line 'weathering lowered tensile modulus from 1.8 GPa to 1.2 GPa' (spec-resin-chemistry.json) is, in the Pilipovic text, the figure for the 50:50 MIXED original/recycled powder; for the 100 % original powder the paper says modulus fell by almost half only in two orientations after natural weathering. Correction of attribution, not of the direction of the effect.
findings.evidence_quote: ageing reduced the initial tensile modulus from 1.8 GPa to 1.2 GPa

findings.claim: Formlabs Tough 1500 Resin V2 TDS publishes outdoor ageing (ASTM D4329 Cycle A, to 1000 h), indoor ageing (ASTM D4459, xenon-arc through-glass) and heat ageing (ASTM D3045, 50 C, up to 6 weeks) as graphs of percent-of-initial elongation, modulus and strength. I could not read values off the graphs.
findings.evidence_quote: Tough 1500 Resin V2 was tested in accelerated outdoor weathering conditions according to ASTM D4329 (Cycle A).

findings.claim: The same TDS states: 'accelerated weathering testing cannot fully represent all aging conditions' and recommends additional outdoor testing for the specific application.
findings.evidence_quote: Please note, accelerated weathering testing cannot fully represent all aging conditions.

findings.claim: A Formlabs staff reply (forum, 2026-07-23) says Tough 1500 V2 has indoor and outdoor ageing data in its TDS but that Tough 1000 has no ageing data. Of the three candidate resins in the earlier design, only Flexible 80A V2 has an indoor-ageing test; none of the resin TDS files I scanned has the Nylon-style numeric outdoor study.
findings.evidence_quote: Unfortunately we don't have aging data on that one

findings.claim: Flexible 80A V2 (the swelling layer in the earlier bilayer design) has a TDS indoor-ageing test (ASTM D4459 Sec 7.2.2) and a heat-ageing test; it states 6 weeks at 50 C 'can be interpreted as approximately 1 year at ambient temperature'. I found no outdoor (D4329) test in that TDS.
findings.evidence_quote: According to the standard, a test time of 6 weeks at 50 C can be interpreted as approximately 1 year at ambient temperature.
findings.value: 6 weeks at 50 C ~ 1 year (ASTM D3045 rule as quoted)

findings.claim: Formlabs support page (Italian text, my translation): SLA parts 'become more brittle and change colour' from 405 nm light and the heat of sunlight, and parts for functional or load-bearing use 'must not be exposed to direct UV light for long periods'. This is the vendor's own caution for stock resins.
findings.evidence_quote: Avviso: Le parti destinate a un uso funzionale o portante non devono essere esposte alla luce UV diretta per lunghi periodi di tempo.

findings.claim: UNRESOLVED: Formlabs describes ASTM D4329 Cycle A as 'Xenon arc' (powder white paper) but its resin TDS says samples were removed from 'QUV' (a fluorescent-UV chamber brand), and the parameters quoted (0.89 W/(m2.nm) at 340 nm, 8 h UV at 60 C black panel, 4 h condensation at 50 C) look like a fluorescent-UV cycle. I could not read the ASTM text (blocked), so which lamp type was used is NOT CONFIRMED.
findings.evidence_quote: 8-hour UV with an uninsulated black panel temperature controlled at 60 °C 4-hour condensation with an uninsulated black panel temperature controlled at 50 °C

findings.claim: Calculation (bm_calc.py): 1000 h of accelerated exposure is 83 twelve-hour cycles and is 0.23 % of a 50-year life counted in raw hours; the 96 h UV test in Cheng 2024 is 0.02 %. Any extrapolation to years needs an acceleration factor that no source here agrees on.

EN ISO 62 gives procedures for water absorbed by plastic specimens 'when immersed in water or when subjected to humid air', and the through-thickness moisture diffusion coefficient 'can be determined' assuming Fickian diffusion (valid for homogeneous materials below Tg). This is the ready-made standard method for the diffusivity that earlier agents could not find for any Formlabs resin; nobody I found has run it on one.
findings.evidence_quote: The “through-the-thickness” moisture diffusion coefficient can be determined for single-phase material by assuming Fickian diffusion behaviour with constant moisture absorption properties through the thickness of the test specimen.

findings.claim: EN ISO 62 also covers humid-air exposure, which is what a façade sees; the earlier agents' immersion-cube numbers (Formlabs 24 h, under 1 % mass) are not the humid-air quantity.
findings.evidence_quote: procedures for determining the amount of water absorbed by plastic specimens of defined dimensions, when immersed in water or when subjected to humid air under controlled conditions

findings.claim: ISO 483 describes small enclosures (under 200 dm3) holding constant relative humidity with saturated salt, glycerol/water or sulfuric acid solutions for conditioning and testing plastics: a desk-scale way to hold a coupon at a known RH without a climate chamber.
findings.evidence_quote: using saturated aqueous salt solutions, glycerol/water solutions or sulfuric acid/water solutions, for conditioning and testing plastics

findings.claim: EN ISO 12571 gives hygroscopic sorption methods (desiccator reference method; climatic chamber) for 'porous building materials and products'; dense printed polymers are not porous, so fit is NOT CONFIRMED.
findings.evidence_quote: This International standard specifies two alternative methods for determining hygroscopic sorption properties of porous building materials and products

findings.claim: EN ISO 12572 gives the cup test for water-vapour permeance/permeability of building products.
findings.evidence_quote: specifies a method based on cup tests for determining the water vapour permeance of building products and the water vapour permeability of building materials under isothermal conditions

findings.claim: EN ISO 15148 gives the short-term liquid water absorption coefficient by partial immersion, to assess capillary uptake from rain on site.
findings.evidence_quote: specifies a method for determining, by partial immersion with no temperature gradient, the short-term liquid water absorption coefficient

findings.claim: EN ISO 10456's temperature and moisture conversion coefficients are valid for mean temperatures 0-30 C and design ambient temperatures -30 to +60 C (scope text), so it does not cover a dark façade element that can exceed 60 C (INFERENCE).
findings.evidence_quote: This International Standard provides conversion coefficients for temperature and for moisture.

findings.claim: EN ISO 13788 (condensation risk) is a simplified method that does not take account of 'the variation of material properties with moisture content', so it cannot model a material whose function is to change with moisture.
findings.evidence_quote: the variation of material properties with moisture content

findings.claim: EN ISO 175 (chemical immersion of plastics) 'only considers testing by immersion of the entire surface' and says it may not suit partial or infrequent wetting.
findings.evidence_quote: It only considers testing by immersion of the entire surface of the test specimen

findings.claim: A real cladding assessment (ETA 20/0062 under EAD 090062-00-0404, a bonded aluminium-faced panel kit) lists these ageing tests: hygrothermal cycles, boiling water 6 h at 90 C, water immersion 500 h at 20 C, freeze-thaw cycles, 2500 h hot dry air at 80 C, UVB-and-water, humidity, salt spray, with pass rule delamination resistance above 75 % of initial value. The hygrothermal cycle parameters are not given in the ETA and I could not fetch the EAD text.
findings.evidence_quote: Decay of delamination resistance after hygrothermal cycles

findings.claim: ETA 20/0062 durability programme includes freeze-thaw cycles.
findings.evidence_quote: Decay of delamination resistance after freeze-thaw cycles

findings.claim: ETA acceptance criterion quoted for the aged panels.
findings.evidence_quote: resistance > 75% initial value

findings.claim: EN ISO 899-1 tensile creep: standard test specimens under set pretreatment, temperature and humidity; for engineering-design data the materials are 'intended to be tested over a broad range of stresses, times and environmental conditions' and extensometers are needed.
findings.evidence_quote: If tensile-creep properties are used for engineering-design purposes, the plastics materials are intended to be tested over a broad range of stresses, times and environmental conditions.

findings.claim: EN ISO 899-2:2024 is the three-point flexural creep method; it is for rigid and semi-rigid plastics and may be unsuitable for some fibre-reinforced materials.
findings.evidence_quote: This document specifies a method for determining the flexural creep of plastics in the form of standard test specimens under specified conditions such as those of pre-treatment, temperature and humidity.

findings.claim: Formlabs creep data exist for three resins as graphs only: Tough 1500 V2 and Tough 2000 V2 at 22 C under 4.0 MPa, Tough 1000 at 22 C under 2.0 MPa, each over 14 days ('ISO 6602' as named by Formlabs; I could not confirm that standard's status). Creep strain values are in the graphs and I could not read them.
findings.evidence_quote: Speciments were tested at 22 C under a 4.0 MPa load. Deflection was measured once a day over the course of 14 days.

findings.claim: Tough 1000 creep condition.
findings.evidence_quote: Speciments were tested at 22 C under a 2.0 MPa load. Deflection was measured over the course of 14 days.

findings.claim: Flame Retardant Resin TDS reports tensile creep (ASTM D2990-17) at 65 C and 1.8 MPa, the only Formlabs creep test I found above room temperature; again a graph.
findings.evidence_quote: Creep resistance measurements of Formlabs materials tested at 65 C and a 1.8 MPa load.

findings.claim: DMA: Tough 1500 V2 has a storage-modulus inflection at 60.8 C and Tg 109.6 C; Tough 2000 V2 inflection 76.96 C, Tg 112.2 C. A sun-heated dark façade element can reach this range (INFERENCE; surface temperatures were not sourced), so 22 C creep data do not cover it.
findings.evidence_quote: A glass transition is observed at 109.6 C, and an inflection of the storage (elastic) modulus is observed at 60.8 C.

findings.claim: Tough 2000 V2 DMA.
findings.evidence_quote: A glass transition is observed at 112.2 C, and an inflection of the storage modulus is observed at 76.96 C.

findings.claim: Rueggeberg and Burgert 2015 loaded wooden humidity bilayers with 100 g and 150 g tip loads in a 9-month field test: 'creep with plastic deformation has been induced by this permanent mechanical loading' yet actuation amplitude hardly fell (calculated curvature loss under 3 %). The only sustained-load check on a humidity-responsive element I found.
findings.evidence_quote: creep with plastic deformation has been induced by this permanent mechanical loading

findings.claim: Cheng 2024 clamped bilayers from the bottom and the top 'to evaluate the effect of self-weight on long-term actuation and potential creep' during 170 cycles; curvature stayed consistent after a slight loss in the first ten cycles.
findings.evidence_quote: To evaluate the effect of self-weight on long-term actuation and potential creep

findings.claim: Impact (material level): ISO 179-1 gives the Charpy impact strength of plastics, a comparison number, not a façade pass criterion.
findings.evidence_quote: This part of ISO 179 specifies a method for determining the Charpy impact strength of plastics under defined conditions.

findings.claim: Impact (element level): EN 14019 sets soft-body impact performance of curtain walling (tested to EN 13049) for areas facing human activity; EN 13830 is the curtain-walling product standard. Neither is written for fixed shading fins; applicability NOT CONFIRMED.
findings.evidence_quote: This European Standard defines performance requirements of curtain walling (excluding ‘glass in building’ which is classified under EN 12600) under soft body impact load criteria

findings.claim: In the worked ETA, hard-body impacts are tested with 0.5, 1.0 and 3.0 kg balls at 1, 3 and 10 J and soft-body impacts at 10 J (3 kg bag) and 60, 300, 400 J (50 kg bag), and the result is expressed as a use category, e.g. category I 'a zone readily accessible at ground level to the public'. Table read from a layout-extracted PDF, so the energy-to-mass pairing is medium confidence.
findings.evidence_quote: FIXbond FR LxH = Hard 1J 0.5 kg

findings.claim: Use category I wording in the ETA.
findings.evidence_quote: (I) A zone readily accessible at ground level to the public and vulnerable to hard body impacts but not subjected to abnormally rough use.

findings.claim: EN 13561 (external blinds and awnings) lists 'brise-soleil' among covered products but states it 'does not cover the wind resistance of non-retractable products, e.g. Dutch awnings and brise-soleil'. So the product standard that names fixed louvres leaves their wind resistance to the structural route.
findings.evidence_quote: This European Standard does not cover the wind resistance of non-retractable products, e.g. Dutch awnings and brise-soleil.

findings.claim: EN 1991-1-4 (wind actions) covers 'elements attached to the structure, e.g. components, cladding units and their fixings'; this is the Eurocode route for wind loads on a shading fin and its fixings. UK National Annex not read.
findings.evidence_quote: elements attached to the structure, e. g. components, cladding units and their fixings

findings.claim: EN 1990 'establishes principles and requirements for the safety, serviceability and durability of structures'. Its design-working-life categories (10, 10-25, 15-30, 50, 100 years) appear only in a secondary web summary I read (Designing Buildings wiki), not in the standard; treat the numbers as unverified.
findings.evidence_quote: EN 1990 establishes principles and requirements for the safety, serviceability and durability of structures

findings.claim: EN 14501 classifies solar protection devices by thermal comfort (solar factor, secondary heat transfer, direct solar transmittance) and visual comfort; it is a performance label, not a durability test.
findings.evidence_quote: the solar factor (total solar energy transmittance)

findings.claim: EN 13659 covers shutters and external venetian blinds fitted to buildings.
findings.evidence_quote: This European Standard specifies the performance requirements for shutters and external venetian blinds intended to be fitted externally to buildings and other construction works.

findings.claim: NO STANDARD FOUND for humidity-responsive (hygromorphic) façade elements. A 2024 review of laboratory tests for adaptive opaque façades reports 'few laboratory tests' and 'notable differences in the set-up configurations and protocols'. That review concerns thermal performance; I read only the research centre's news summary, not the paper.
findings.evidence_quote: Few laboratory tests characterized adaptive opaque facades' thermal performance and moreover, reported tests have notable differences in the set-up configurations and protocols.

findings.claim: How the published humidity-responsive work is evaluated (Cheng 2024): climate chamber at 10, 20 and 30 C with RH in 10 % steps from 15 to 95 %, 2 h per step, curvature from time-lapse images; a cyclic test 90 % RH for 120 min then 30 % RH for 240 min.
findings.evidence_quote: The bilayer specimens were exposed to several permutations of temperature (10 ∘ C, 20 ∘ C, and 30 ∘ C) and RH (in steps of 10% from 15–95% RH

findings.claim: Same paper, cycle definition.
findings.evidence_quote: programmed to cycle between 90% RH for 120 minutes and 30% RH for 240 minutes

findings.claim: Calculation: 170 cycles of 6 h = 1020 h = 42.5 days; one RH cycle per day for 25 years is 9125 cycles, so 170 is 1.9 % of that (bm_calc.py). The authors report 170 cycles with consistent curvature at 30 % RH after a slight loss in the first ten at 90 % RH.
findings.evidence_quote: For all 170 tested actuation cycles, the bilayers display consistent curvatures at the low RH of 30%.

findings.claim: Temperature matters as much as humidity for the evaluation: at 30 C the bilayers had almost no curvature at the lowest RH while at 10 C they kept 0.011 /mm, so a humidity test at one temperature does not characterise the element.
findings.evidence_quote: At a higher temperature of 30 ∘ C, the cellulosic bilayers are observed to have almost no curvature at the lowest RH values.

findings.claim: Field evidence for wood bilayers: a 9-month outdoor test at ETH Zurich started July 2013.
findings.evidence_quote: The experiment started in July 2013 and ran for nine months.

findings.claim: Rueggeberg and Burgert note that mechanical load 'may cause creep in the viscoelastic wood elements with severe impact on the actuation capability', listing creep as a failure mode to test.
findings.evidence_quote: Mechanical load may cause creep in the viscoelastic wood elements with severe impact on the actuation capability.

findings.claim: Project-record check (bm_calc.py, grid 0.05-20 in m and n): the Timoshenko coefficient f(m,n) never exceeds 1.5 and equals 1.500000000000 at m^2 n = 1 for m = 0.5, 1, 2, 3.7. This agrees with the Lean-checked ceiling; it is a numerical re-check, not a new proof.

Formlabs TDS coefficients of thermal expansion (0-150 C, ASTM E831) are large and differ widely: Rigid 10K about 41-48, Tough 1500 V2 99-116, Tough 2000 V2 134-143, Tough 1000 162-168 (the TDS text shows the unit as 'm/m/C'; the micro sign was lost in extraction, and the BioMed Durable TDS prints 'um/m/C'). Which column is green or post-cured is not read.
findings.evidence_quote: Thermal Expansion (0-150 C) 161.6

findings.claim: Rigid 10K CTE row.
findings.evidence_quote: Thermal Expansion, 0-150 C 48

findings.claim: Tough 1500 V2 CTE row.
findings.evidence_quote: Thermal Expansion (0-150 C) 116

findings.claim: CALCULATION: a Rigid 10K / Tough 1000 bilayer, the low-water-uptake pair the earlier agents proposed as passive layer plus stiff control, has a differential CTE of 113.6-127.2 um/m/C. Over a 40 K swing (20 to 60 C, my assumed range) that is a differential thermal strain of 0.45-0.51 %, which is 2.3-2.5 times the 0.2 % hygroscopic differential strain the earlier agent ESTIMATED for 24 h in stock resins. At the Lean-checked optimum (kappa = 1.5 d_eps / h) and h = 1 mm that is a curvature of 0.0068-0.0076 per mm (radius 131-147 mm) from temperature alone. Because the CTE was averaged over 0-150 C, across the glass transition, it probably overstates the glassy-range value; the ratio is an order-of-magnitude warning, not a prediction.

Implication for evaluation (INFERENCE): any humidity test of a printed bilayer must hold temperature constant and report it, and a thermal-only control (dry, ramped temperature) is needed, because thermal bimorph bending can match or exceed the hygroscopic signal. Cheng 2024 already shows a strong temperature effect on humidity-driven curvature.

VS EARLIER (spec-formlabs-materials.json, 18 SLA resins): that table omits Formlabs' Flame Retardant Resin, which is on formlabs.com in the Form 4 family list. It is UL 94 V-0 at 3 mm, HDT 83 C (1.8 MPa), Tg 144 C (post-cured 80 C/120 min), tensile modulus 3.1 GPa. So the catalogue was not complete for the fire question. Its CTE (20-80 C, ASTM E831/E813 as printed) is 98.6 and 68.1 um/m/C (two columns, state mapping not read).
findings.evidence_quote: Coefficient of Thermal Expansion, 20- 80C 98.6

findings.claim: VS EARLIER (spec-architecture-gaps.json): that file notes 'UL 94 HB' for Nylon 11 Pro. HB at 3 mm is not special to that powder: it is the Formlabs rating for Rigid 10K, Tough 1000/1500/2000 (post-cured) and all Nylon 12 variants read here. Only Flame Retardant Resin is better, and only at 3 mm.
findings.evidence_quote: Testing Standard Rating UL 94 Section 7 HB

findings.claim: VS EARLIER (spec-resin-chemistry.json: 'I did not retrieve a quantitative UV-ageing study for Formlabs resins'): true for resins' numbers, but Formlabs does publish ageing curves in resin TDS files (Tough 1500 V2 outdoor/indoor/heat; Flexible 80A V2 indoor/heat) and a numeric 1000 h D4329 study for two nylon powders. The resin values are in graphs I could not read, so the gap on numbers stays open.
findings.evidence_quote: Tough 1500 Resin V2 was tested in accelerated outdoor weathering conditions according to ASTM D4329 (Cycle A).

findings.claim: VS EARLIER: the earlier materials were chosen for low water uptake (Rigid 10K, Tough 1000, Silicone 40A as passive layers). Water uptake is the wrong single screen for a façade element; creep at temperature, CTE mismatch (above) and UV are each the same size or larger problems and are not in the earlier selection logic.

RECOMMENDATION (my synthesis, not from a source): a desk-scale printed demonstrator legitimately escapes the Building Regulations, the Construction Products Regulation (no DoP/CE/UKCA), Euroclass SBI testing, wind and impact categories, and a stated design working life. It does not escape honest statements: it should say 'not fire classified; UL 94 HB (or V-0 if FR resin, 3 mm only); not weather-tested beyond what is reported'.

RECOMMENDATION (proof of concept, small coupons, all within a desk lab): (1) EN ISO 62 water uptake and diffusion in immersion and in humid air, at fixed temperature; (2) ISO 483 salt-solution RH chambers; (3) cyclic RH like Cheng 2024 (90/30 % RH, 6 h cycle, 170+ cycles) at 3 temperatures plus a dry thermal-only control; (4) EN ISO 4892-3 or -2 exposure of at least 96 h (the published floor) up to 1000 h (the Formlabs powder precedent), then re-measure curvature and modulus; (5) ISO 899-1/-2 creep at 22 C and a hot temperature near the DMA inflection; (6) ISO 1182 cylinders and ISO 1716 for non-combustibility/PCS screening, labelled as screening.

RECOMMENDATION (installation, e.g. a pavilion shown by the architecture practice): the relevant gates are Regulation 7 and ADB if attached to a building; Schedule 2 temporary-building exemption (28 days) if freestanding and short-lived; the venue's fire risk assessment (Regulatory Reform (Fire Safety) Order 2005, NOT researched here); and wind and fixing design to EN 1991-1-4. An early conversation with building control and a fire engineer is the only way to settle which applies. NOT CONFIRMED.

RECOMMENDATION (product): a facade element would need (a) a declared reaction-to-fire class from EN 13501-1 testing of the element as mounted (SBI wings, 3 specimens); if on a relevant building at 18 m or more and above 4.5 m, A2-s1,d0, which in all likelihood needs a mineral-filled or inorganic design (INFERENCE); (b) a durability programme like the ETA list (hygrothermal cycles, freeze-thaw, 500 h water, 2500 h heat, UV-and-water, retention above 75 %); (c) impact category; (d) wind to EN 1991-1-4; (e) a stated design working life; (f) the UK conformity route (UKCA/BBA), which I did not research.

UNVERIFIED BACKGROUND (not load-bearing): organic printable polymers such as PA12 and acrylate resins typically have heats of combustion of tens of MJ/kg, far above the 3.0 MJ/kg A2 limit. I could not fetch a primary table (FAA server returned 503), so I do not use this number anywhere above.

key_claims.claim: In England a 'relevant building' (a storey at least 18 m up, with dwellings, an institution or residential rooms) must use only Euroclass A2-s1,d0 or A1 materials in external walls and specified attachments, and the slats of a solar shading device are not exempt (only non-shading components are); shading devices up to 4.5 m above ground are outside the rule. This is the single hardest legal gate for a polymer shading element.
key_claims.evidence_quote: components associated with a solar shading device excluding components whose primary function is to provide shade or deflect sunlight such as the awning curtain or slats

key_claims.claim: Euroclass classification (EN 13501-1) is made on the product in end use with large specimens (SBI: wings 495 x 1500 mm and (1000+t) x 1500 mm, at least 3 specimens), so a desk-scale print cannot be classified; Formlabs publishes only UL 94 (HB at 3 mm where a rating is given, which is 9 of 25 data sheets scanned; V-0 at 3 mm, V-1 at 2.5 mm, HB at 1.5 mm for Flame Retardant Resin), and UL 94 does not occur in Approved Document B.

No standard exists for evaluating humidity-responsive façade elements; the published practice is a bespoke chamber protocol (Cheng 2024: 170 cycles of 90/30 % RH at 6 h per cycle, 96 h of ISO 4892 UV at 60 C, 10/20/30 C RH matrix). The nearest England-wide wording is Approved Document 7 para 1.27: residual properties of property-changing materials must be estimatable and adequate for the expected life.
key_claims.evidence_quote: Materials that are susceptible to changes in their properties may be used in building work and will meet the requirements of the regulations if the residual properties, including the structural properties, meet both of the following conditions.

key_claims.claim: For the earlier stock-Formlabs bilayer design, temperature is as large a driver as humidity: Formlabs-published CTEs differ by 114-127 um/m/C between Rigid 10K and Tough 1000, giving 0.45-0.51 % differential strain over 40 K versus the earlier agent's estimated 0.2 % hygroscopic strain (own calculation, bm_calc.py). Creep and ageing data from Formlabs exist only at 22 C or as unreadable graphs, while the DMA storage modulus of Tough 1500 V2 starts to fall at 60.8 C.
key_claims.evidence_quote: A glass transition is observed at 109.6 C, and an inflection of the storage (elastic) modulus is observed at 60.8 C.

could_not_find: ISO.org, ASTM.org and ANSI webstore returned HTTP 403 to every fetch: the text of ISO 7892, ASTM D4329, D4459, D3045, D2990, D256, G154, G155 and the ISO 4892 clauses was not read. Scope statements came from the Estonian standards body (evs.ee), a Czech reseller, Efectis and Formlabs documents.

EAD 090062-00-0404 / 090062-01-0404 text (kits for external wall claddings): connection reset on the only copy found. Hygrothermal-cycle parameters (temperatures, humidity, number of cycles) and the exact impact test procedure are therefore not stated; only the list of tests and acceptance wording from one ETA.
BR 135, BS 8414-1/-2, ISO 7892 numbers, EN 13823 clause text and EN ISO 11925-2 specimen size: paywalled or not fetched.

UK conformity route for products (Construction Products Regulations 2013 as retained, UKCA marking, BBA): not read. Scotland, Wales (Welsh Regulation 7 differs) and Northern Ireland rules not researched; the Regulatory Reform (Fire Safety) Order 2005 and event/venue fire safety not researched.
EN 1990 Table 2.1 design working life values from a primary source: only a secondary web summary was seen (low confidence); the UK National Annex was not read.
Any EN 13501-1 class for any Formlabs resin or powder, for the architecture practice's PLA modules, or for any printed hygromorph.

A primary polymer heat-of-combustion table (FAA report server returned 503, rosap returned 403), so no number to compare against the 3.0 MJ/kg A2 limit; the statement that organic printable polymers cannot reach A2 is reasoning, not a measured result.
Values from the Formlabs ageing, creep and DMA graphs (percent-of-initial curves, creep strain after 14 days) are figures; I could not read numbers off them.
Formlabs CTE units and which column is green or post-cured; the micro sign was lost in text extraction.
Whether Formlabs' ASTM D4329 test used xenon-arc or fluorescent UV (their documents disagree); the date of the Formlabs nylon weathering white paper.
ISO 6602 (the standard Formlabs names for its flexural creep test): status not confirmed; ISO 899-2:2024 is the current flexural creep standard per the Estonian standards board listing.
Surface temperatures reached by dark polymer façade elements in UK sun (no sourced figure); the 60 C and 40 K ranges in calculations are assumptions.

Juaristi et al. 2024 full text and the 'Structural characterisation of adaptive facades in Europe, Part II' paper: only secondary summaries were seen. No cycle-count or pass-fail standard for actuated or humidity-responsive façade elements was found, which is an absence in my search, not proof none exists.
A humid-air water uptake or hygroscopic expansion measurement for any Formlabs resin or powder, still absent after this run (as in earlier agents).

glossary.plain: The European A1 to F grade for how much a building product helps a fire grow; A1 is best.
Almost non-burning (A2), very little smoke (s1) and no burning drips (d0).
A fire test where a two-wall corner of the product, about 1.5 m tall, is burned and the heat and smoke are measured.
A small-flame plastics test (HB, V-2, V-1, V-0) from the electronics world; it is not a building grade.
UK government guidance on how to meet the Building Regulations; following it is accepted as compliance but is not the only way.
In England, a building with a storey at least 18 m up that contains homes, an institution or residential rooms.
A part fixed to an outer wall, such as a balcony, solar panel or shading device, that follows the same fire rule as the wall.
A material that changes shape when the air humidity changes, like a pine cone scale.
Two layers stuck together that expand by different amounts, so the strip bends.
How damp the air is, as a percentage of the most water it could hold at that temperature.
Slow sagging of a plastic under a steady load.
The temperature range where a hard plastic turns rubbery; DMA is the test that shows it.
Coefficient of thermal expansion: how much a material grows per degree of warming.
A family of lab methods that age plastics with lamps, heat and water spray to imitate sunlight and rain.
How fast water soaks into a material.
Technical data sheet: the maker's own table of test results.
European Technical Assessment and the assessment document it follows; a route to approve a product that has no standard.
Labels showing a product meets the legal route for being sold for building use in the UK or EU.

recommendations: State the fire position on every PoC label: not Euroclass tested; UL 94 HB at 3 mm for stock resins and nylon, V-0 only for Flame Retardant Resin at 3 mm and not at flap thickness.
Run EN ISO 62 on the chosen layer resins in immersion and humid air, at one fixed temperature, to get the water diffusion coefficient no earlier agent found.
Add a dry thermal-only control (ramp 20 to 60 C) to the humidity test of any stock-resin bilayer; use the measured differential CTE, not water uptake alone, to choose the passive layer.

Use the Cheng 2024 protocol as a floor (90/30 % RH, 6 h cycle, 170 cycles, three temperatures, 96 h ISO 4892 UV) and report curvature drift per cycle; extend to 1000 h UV (Formlabs precedent) before claiming outdoor use.
Test creep of the actual bilayer under its own weight at 22 C and at a temperature near the DMA inflection (about 60 C for Tough 1500 V2); do not rely on the 22 C Formlabs curves.

Screen small printed cylinders with ISO 1182 and ISO 1716 if a non-combustible claim is ever considered, labelled as screening. If the aim is a building product, plan for a mineral-filled or inorganic design or limit use to heights up to 4.5 m or non-relevant buildings, and confirm with building control.
Before any installation, ask building control and a fire engineer which gate applies (Regulation 7, Schedule 2 28-day exemption, venue fire risk assessment); this report cannot settle it.
Get the paywalled texts (ISO 7892, ASTM D4329/D4459/D3045/D2990, EAD 090062-01-0404, BR 135, BS 8414) before quoting them to the partner.
